Chapter 3 • Topological Manifolds

3.1 Topological Spaces

  • The powerset \(\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})\) of a set \(\mathcal{M}\) is the set of all possible subsets of \(\mathcal{M}\).

  • The set \(\mathcal{O}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\mathcal{M})\) defines a topology on \(\mathcal{M}\), denoted as \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\), if and only if:

    1. The topology contains the empty set and the whole space itself: \(\emptyset \in \mathcal{O}\) and \(\mathcal{M} \in \mathcal{O}\),

    2. The intersection of any two sets that belong to the topology, \(\mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V}\in \mathcal{O}\) (referred to as open sets), is also an open set: \(\forall \mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O} \rightarrow \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O}\).

    3. Any union of open sets (even an infinite one) is also an open set: \(\bigcup_{\alpha}\mathcal{U}_{\alpha}\in \mathcal{O}\), where \(\alpha\) denotes an arbitrary index set.

    A set \(\mathcal{C} \subseteq \mathcal{M}\) is said to be closed under the topology \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\) if its complement is open: \(\mathcal{C} \text{ is closed} \iff \mathcal{M} \setminus \mathcal{C} \in \mathcal{O}\). Note that a set can be open, closed, both (clopen), or neither, depending on the topology.

  • The doublet \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}\right)\) is a topological space.

  • Given a topological space \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\), the inherited topology (or subspace topology) on a subset \(\mathcal{N} \subseteq \mathcal{M}\) is defined as \begin{align*} \left.\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}}\right|_{\mathcal{M}} \coloneqq \left\lbrace \mathcal{N} \cap \mathcal{U} : \mathcal{U} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right\rbrace. \end{align*} That is, a subset \(\mathcal{V} \subseteq \mathcal{N}\) is declared open in \(\mathcal{N}\) if and only if it can be written as the intersection of \(\mathcal{N}\) with an open set \(\mathcal{U}\) from the ambient topology \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\).

  • The \(\mathbb{R}^d\) standard topology, \(\mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\), is \begin{align*} \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d} \coloneqq \Big\{\mathcal{U} \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \;\Big|\; \forall p \in \mathcal{U}\;\exists r>0:\; B_r(p) \subseteq \mathcal{U}\Big\}, \end{align*} where the soft/open ball of radius \(r\) about \(p=(p_1,\dots,p_d)\) is \[ B_r(p) \coloneqq \Big\{ q=(q_1,\dots,q_d)\in\mathbb{R}^d \;\Big|\; \sum_{i=1}^d (q_i-p_i)^2 < r^2\Big\}. \]

  • A topological space \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) is Hausdorff if any two distinct points can be separated by disjoint open sets: \begin{align*} \forall \, p, q \in \mathcal{M}, \; p \neq q, \;\; \exists \, \mathcal{U}, \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} : \; p \in \mathcal{U}, \; q \in \mathcal{V}, \; \mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \emptyset. \end{align*} For instance, \(\left(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\right)\) is Hausdorff: take two open balls centred at \(p\) and \(q\), of radius half their distance.

  • The map \(\phi: \mathcal{M} \rightarrow \mathcal{N}\) is continuous w.r.t. \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) and \(\left(\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}}\right)\) if and only if the preimage of every open set in the target space \(\mathcal{N}\) is also an open set in the domain \(\mathcal{M}\), i.e. \begin{align*} \forall \mathcal{V} \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \rightarrow \mathrm{preim}_{\phi}(\mathcal{V}) \coloneqq \left\lbrace p \in \mathcal{M} \mid \phi(p) \in \mathcal{V}\right\rbrace \in \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}. \end{align*} This encodes the idea that \(\phi\) does not “tear” or “break” the underlying topological structure.

  • Given two topological spaces \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\), a map \(\phi \colon \mathcal{M} \longrightarrow \mathcal{N}\), is a homeomorphism w.r.t. \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\) – if and only if:

    1. \(\phi\) is bijective, hence invertible, i.e. there exists an inverse map: \(\phi^{-1} \colon \mathcal{N} \longrightarrow \mathcal{M}\).

    2. \(\phi\) is continuous w.r.t. \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\).

    3. \(\phi^{-1}\) is also continuous w.r.t. \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{N}} \right)\) and \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\).

  • A topological space \(\left(\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\right)\) is second countable if its topology admits a countable basis, i.e. a countable collection \(\mathcal{B} \subseteq \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}}\) such that every open set is a union of elements of \(\mathcal{B}\). For instance, the open balls with rational centres and rational radii form a countable basis of \(\left(\mathbb{R}^d, \mathcal{O}_{\mathbb{R}^d}\right)\).
